name: Parsnip
summary: Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa) is a cool-season storage-root crop. Established plants need deep, loose soil and steady moisture; cool fall conditions can improve root quality. Harvest cues and pest signs are described at species/crop scope, not as cultivar-specific guarantees.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Pastinaca sativa. This profile represents the crop species, not a named cultivar such as Hollow Crown.

growth.short: Biennial storage root that develops through cool weather
growth.guidance: Kew describes Pastinaca sativa as biennial. USU Extension identifies parsnip as a cool-season root crop and reports poorer growth and flavor quality in high summer heat; several weeks of cool weather can improve flavor. This is species/crop-level context, not a cultivar-specific maturity promise.

cultivation.short: Sunny site with deep, loose, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: USU Extension recommends a sunny site and fertile, deep, well-drained soil for established parsnips. Light soil favors straighter roots; heavy soil may need deeper preparation and organic matter. This is outdoor soil guidance, not a container-size or hydroponic recipe.

maintenance.short: Keep root-zone moisture steady as the crop develops
maintenance.guidance: USU gives about 1–2 inches of water per week depending on weather and soil, and warns that moisture swings can contribute to cracking, bitterness and other root disorders. Treat the amount as regional outdoor guidance; mulch can help conserve soil moisture. Seedling thinning and direct-sowing instructions remain in the Seed Profile.

harvest.short: Lift full-size roots after cool weather; loosen soil first
harvest.guidance: USU Extension recommends harvesting when roots reach full size and loosening the soil with a digging fork before lifting. Cool fall conditions can improve flavor; roots may remain under heavy mulch, but should be harvested before spring regrowth makes them woody. Its 100–120-day estimate is not a guarantee for every variety or site.

problems.short: Watch for root tunneling, wet-weather leaf blights and decay
problems.guidance: USU Extension describes parsnip-fly larvae as small white maggots feeding in roots, and leaf blights as spots associated with foliage staying wet for long periods. Root rots or spots can cause decay or forked-looking roots. These are observation cues, not a diagnosis or pesticide recommendation.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected evidence addresses a taproot crop in deep soil and does not establish a Garden system configuration.

growthHabits.reason: The compatibility vocabulary does not describe taproot crop architecture.

spacing.reason: Outdoor row spacing is not converted to system positions.

light.reason: Outdoor garden guidance is not converted to indoor grow-light tiers.

name: Rutabaga
variety: Rutabaga crop type; no cultivar assigned
summary: Rutabaga is a root-crop type within Brassica napus, distinct from turnip (Brassica rapa). It is a slow, cool-season crop commonly harvested in autumn; its swollen root and leaves are both usable, with regional harvest cues kept separate from cultivar-specific claims.

identity.short: Rutabaga crop type within Brassica napus
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Brassica napus at species level; USU Extension treats rutabaga as a crop type and lists rutabaga varieties separately. No named cultivar or infraspecific taxon is assigned here.

growth.short: Slow-growing cool-season crop with an enlarged root
growth.guidance: USU Extension describes rutabaga as slower to mature than turnip and generally grown for fall harvest. UMN likewise distinguishes rutabaga (Brassica napus) from turnip (Brassica rapa) and notes that cool weather favors quality. Timing remains crop-level and regional, not a cultivar date.

cultivation.short: Direct sow for a cool-season harvest in deep, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: USU recommends direct sowing into deep, fertile, well-drained soil and summer planting for fall harvest in its Utah context. UMN gives a late-May-to-early-June window for Minnesota. These dates are regional soil-garden guidance and are not converted to indoor timing or hydroponic suitability.

maintenance.short: Keep growth steady; avoid drought and water swings
maintenance.guidance: USU recommends regular, uniform moisture and notes fluctuations can contribute to cracked, woody or pithy roots. UMN reports drought stress can make rutabagas bitter or woody. Both sources discuss outdoor soil production; they do not establish a Garden pod count or recirculating-system recipe.

harvest.short: Harvest roots after cool weather; leaves are also usable
harvest.guidance: USU gives about 4 inches in root diameter as a rutabaga harvest cue and describes maturity over a broad crop window. UMN notes frost can improve flavor and that rutabagas may remain in the ground into autumn where soil conditions permit. Both cues vary by region and cultivar; UMN also says mature leaves can be harvested. No universal calendar date is assigned.

uses.short: The swollen root and mature leaves are edible
uses.guidance: UMN Extension identifies rutabaga roots and leaves as edible and discusses long-term storage of roots under root-cellar conditions. These crop-use notes do not establish a cultivar-specific flavor profile or health benefit.

problems.short: Heat, drought and insect pressure affect crop quality
problems.guidance: USU and UMN describe heat or uneven moisture as quality risks, including woody, bitter or pithy roots. UMN also lists flea beetles and root maggots among turnip/rutabaga pests. These are crop-level concerns, not claims of disease susceptibility or resistance for an unrepresented cultivar.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The evidence is for root development in soil and does not establish system suitability.

growthHabits.reason: Root-crop form is not represented by the controlled compatibility habit vocabulary.

spacing.reason: Field spacing is not translated into system pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor sun guidance is not converted to an indoor light tier.

name: Hyacinth Bean
summary: Hyacinth bean is a vigorous twining ornamental legume with showy flowers and purple pods. Give the established vine a sunny, moist but well-drained site and sturdy support. Young pods are edible only when cooked; mature seeds require careful preparation because the species has toxic characteristics.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Lablab purpureus and lists Dolichos purpureus as a synonym. Hyacinth bean is the species-level ornamental/food crop here; no named cultivar is assigned.

growth.short: Twining vine with showy flowers and colorful pods
growth.guidance: NCSU describes a twining vine with purple stems and late-summer flowers followed by colorful pods. Published mature-height ranges differ: Illinois reports growth up to 30 ft, while NCSU lists 10–25 ft. Treat it as a vigorous vine requiring substantial vertical space, not a fixed Garden-system dimension.

cultivation.short: Full sun, moist but well-drained soil, and frost-free establishment
cultivation.guidance: NCSU recommends sun, light moist well-drained soil, a sturdy trellis, and planting after frost danger has passed; it notes good performance in hot, humid climates. These are outdoor landscape conditions, not indoor-light or hydroponic settings.

maintenance.short: Train the vigorous vine on sturdy support
maintenance.guidance: NCSU specifically recommends a sturdy trellis to carry the vine's weight. Illinois describes vigorous climbing growth; neither source gives a routine pruning schedule, so do not impose one as a species requirement.

harvest.short: Pick young pods while tender; do not treat mature seeds like ordinary beans
harvest.guidance: NCSU reports purple pods around 2–4 inches and says young immature pods can be cooked and eaten. UMN Extension advises harvesting green pods while juicy and tender and cooking hyacinth bean because seeds can contain toxins. Mature dried seeds require thorough boiling with repeated water changes according to NCSU; this is a safety caution, not a complete recipe.

uses.short: Ornamental flowers and pods; food use requires careful cooking
uses.guidance: NCSU describes hyacinth bean as commonly grown ornamentally in the United States, while documenting food use of young pods and mature seeds in other regions. Young pods are cooked; mature dried seeds need thorough boiling and multiple water changes. Do not infer that all plant parts are safe to eat or apply a preservation recipe from this profile.

problems.short: Food safety: raw pods and mature seeds require caution
problems.guidance: NCSU flags toxic characteristics associated with cyanogenic glycosides, especially in mature seeds, and reports low-severity poison characteristics; follow its thorough-cooking and repeated-water-change caution rather than eating raw pods or seeds. No cultivar-specific disease or pest resistance is established.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The sources describe a vigorous outdoor climbing ornamental, not Garden system performance.

growthHabits.reason: The compatibility schema has no climbing-vine value; habit is described in the Plant Profile.

spacing.reason: No outdoor vine spacing is converted into system positions.

light.reason: Full-sun garden advice is not an indoor grow-light classification.

name: Winged Bean
summary: Winged bean is a tropical climbing legume recognized by four ruffled ridges on its pods. It needs heat, moisture during dry weather, and a trellis; traditional short-day types may flower poorly outside suitable daylengths. Young pods are harvested very small, and the crop is valued for several edible plant parts in regions where it is commonly grown.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Psophocarpus tetragonolobus. UF/IFAS identifies winged bean by its climbing habit and four longitudinal pod wings; common names such as goa bean are search aliases, not separate identities.

growth.short: Climbing tropical legume with distinctive winged pods
growth.guidance: UF/IFAS describes a climbing plant with weak vining stems and pods bearing four angled wings. It notes daylength sensitivity in traditional types and availability of day-neutral cultivars; no particular cultivar is represented here.

cultivation.short: Heat-loving crop with regional seasonal limits
cultivation.guidance: UF/IFAS reports winged bean as suited to hot, humid Florida conditions, sensitive to frost, and requiring irrigation in dry weather. Those conditions do not establish suitability in every home garden or hydroponic system.

maintenance.short: Provide a trellis and avoid drying stress
maintenance.guidance: UF/IFAS says the weak-rooted climbing plant should have a trellis or other support in place before growth and that winged bean is not drought tolerant. Keep the support strong and monitor moisture during dry weather; the source does not establish a pruning schedule or Garden pod layout.

harvest.short: Pick young pods at about 2–4 inches for tender use
harvest.guidance: UF/IFAS gives 2–4 inches as the harvest size for young pods and notes that mature pods can reach 6–9 inches. Mature seeds have a harder shell and need longer cooking than common beans; these sizes describe the UF/IFAS source, not a cultivar-specific calendar or yield.

uses.short: Pods, leaves and flowers are used as food in its home-growing regions
uses.guidance: UF/IFAS describes young pods prepared like snap beans and reports that leaves, flowers and roots are also eaten in parts of southern Asia and the Pacific. Some varieties are specifically selected for tuberous roots; this unspecified identity does not promise root yield or a root-selected cultivar. Mature beans require longer cooking because of their hard shells.

problems.short: Frost, drought and daylength can limit flowering or production
problems.guidance: UF/IFAS reports frost sensitivity and lack of drought tolerance. Traditional short-day types may not initiate flowers under unsuitable daylength, while day-neutral cultivars are available; this profile represents no such cultivar, so flowering response remains selection- and region-dependent. No disease resistance is claimed.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The cited cultivation source addresses warm-region soil production, not hydroponic performance.

growthHabits.reason: Vining habit is documented but the controlled compatibility profile does not represent trellised tropical legumes.

spacing.reason: Field support and spacing are not converted to indoor system positions.

light.reason: Sunny outdoor exposure is not equated with an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Pineapple Sage
summary: Pineapple sage is the accepted Salvia elegans species, a tender perennial subshrub grown for aromatic foliage and late-season red flowers. Extension sources differ in emphasis: one cautions against routine seed growing, while another notes seed and cutting routes; named cultivars should be preserved vegetatively.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Salvia elegans. The profile is species-level and does not assign cultivars such as Golden Delicious or Honey Melon, which have distinct vegetative selection traits.

growth.short: Tender perennial subshrub with late flowers
growth.guidance: Kew characterizes the species as a subshrub. UW–Madison Extension describes an open, upright plant with late-season scarlet flowers; it may be grown as an annual in colder climates and can die back after frost.

cultivation.guidance: UW–Madison Extension recommends full sun and moist, well-drained soil, noting leaf drop or wilting when plants dry out. Its regional overwintering guidance depends on local climate; no hydroponic suitability is inferred.

maintenance.short: Pinch young plants; remove old wood when regrowth begins
maintenance.guidance: UW–Madison Extension says pinching young pineapple sage encourages branching and denser growth; old woody shoots can be removed when new growth appears. It also notes tall stems can be vulnerable to wind damage.

harvest.short: Leaves and flowers have culinary and ornamental uses
harvest.guidance: UW–Madison Extension describes the leaves and flowers as edible and suggests using young leaves fresh; NCSU Extension also describes edible flowers. Use correctly identified plants and ordinary food-handling practices; no medicinal effects are claimed.

propagation.short: Seed is possible; cuttings retain named selections
propagation.guidance: UW–Madison Extension says the species can be grown from seed but cultivars are propagated from tip cuttings. NCSU advises against seed growing unless starts are raised indoors and planted out as established plants. These sources differ in recommendation strength, so seed use is possible but vegetative material is preferred for named cultivars.

problems.short: Drought and late flowering can limit performance
problems.guidance: UW–Madison Extension reports wilting, leaf curl or leaf drop when too dry and notes that flowering may occur late enough to be cut short by frost in colder regions. Greenhouse pests are not generalized to every outdoor plant.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected sources describe garden and container cultivation, not a hydroponic production trial.

growthHabits.reason: Subshrub habit does not map to the compatibility profile's supported growth-habit categories.

height.reason: UW–Madison reports species range and cultivar variation; no representative mature dimension selected.

spread.reason: UW–Madison reports species range and cultivar variation; no representative mature dimension selected.
